newsitem.title: GERMANY: New German insurer seen as strong Allianz rival.
newsitem.headline: New German insurer seen as strong Allianz rival.

text.p: The surprise mega-merger in the German insurance industry will create a significant rival for the market leader Allianz AG, outranking the Munich giant in several key areas, analysts said on Friday.

The merger announced overnight will fuse reinsurer Munich Re's Hamburg-Mannheimer AG subsidiary with Victoria Holding AG, a leading non-life insurer, to create the country's second largest primary insurance company.

Munich Re, which has a cross-shareholding agreement and longstanding historical ties with Allianz, will own between 55 and 60 percent of the new company, which will be called ERGO and have annual sales of some 21 billion marks.
A valuation procedure for Victoria and Hamburg-Mannheimer later this year will fix the ratio of their contributions to the ERGO group and the level of control Munich Re will have.
Analysts said the merger was an ideal blend of strengths in different segments of the insurance industry.

Victoria is a composite insurer and includes Europe's leading legal protection insurer D.A.S. while Hamburg-Mannheimer includes DKV, the market leader in European health insurance which Munich Re acquired last year.
The deal was also viewed as a sensible way for Munich Re to gain a stronger role in primary insurance without a costly outright takeover.
Munich Re owns 80 percent of Hamburg-Mannheimer and already has an 18 percent direct stake in Victoria as well as an indirect stake of 5.3 percent.
"This is a great solution," said Patrizia Novak, insurance analyst at Commerzbank AG in Frankfurt.
"We don't have full details yet but it appears that Munich Re is getting a stronger position in primary insurance without actually having to spend."
"The new group is really an ideal mix," said Georg Kanders, head of insurance research at WestLB in Duesseldorf.
"It has strengths in a wide range of sectors. Victoria is mainly focused on non-life, Hamburg-Mannheimer on life and with the DKV as a strong name in health insurance, this is a very strong group."
"This will balance out Munich Re's business in general. Reinsurance is a cyclical business, and primary insurance less so," Kanders added.
The precise financial implications of the deal are unclear since the valuations have yet to take place.

Munich Re said the merger would boost its group premium income by some 8.4 billion marks to about 46.6 billion marks due to the consolidation of its Victoria stake and add some five marks to its earnings per share.
The extent of synergy effects is unclear.
Most analysts said they were keeping their recommendations on the participants in the deal unchanged for the moment.
Commerzbank's Novak, who has a "neutral" recommendation on Munich Re, said she viewed the shares as overpriced, despite her appreciation of its strategy.
An analysts' meeting on the deal has been scheduled for Monday in Frankfurt.
The immediate reaction on the stock market was a burst of interest in Munich Re shares, which surged to trade up 425 marks, or nine percent at 5,340 marks mid-way through the bourse session.
Victoria shares were up 25 marks at 1,825.
Allianz shares, meanwhile, were also higher at 388.70 marks, up 20.20 marks, or 5.5 percent.

Allianz, which owns 25 percent of Munich Re in a cross-sharholding deal, said it expected tougher competition ahead after the merger but welcomed the move as a logical response to deregulation in the European insurance sector.

The merger, which has yet to be approved by the German Federal Cartel Office and by shareholders, follows the fusion of UAP and Axa of France announced last November which ousted Allianz from the position of Europe's biggest insurer.
